standard.title: Explore language features
standard.description: explore, with support, language features of the target language noticing similarities and differences between the target language and English
standard.prior_knowledge: Foundation students bring home-based familiarity with the target language — spoken sounds, phrases and vocabulary — but have not yet formally examined it as a system. They bring developing awareness of English from their school environment. They have not previously been asked to compare the two languages, notice structural features, or describe how languages work.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students notice and explore features of the target language — including sounds, writing conventions and basic word patterns — and identify simple similarities and differences between the target language and English with support.

nodes.label: Noticing sounds and pronunciation features
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can notice and imitate distinctive sounds, rhythms and intonation patterns in the target language, and identify ways these differ from English.
nodes.minimum_width: Imitate at least two sounds or sound patterns from the target language and identify whether they are the same as or different from English sounds.
nodes.typical_width: Explore and imitate the sound system of the target language — including distinctive vowels, consonants and tonal or rhythmic features; compare with English sound patterns; participate in songs, rhymes and chants that highlight sound features.
wider: Compare animal sounds, counting rhymes or familiar expressions across the target language and English — identify where the sounds are shared, similar or distinctly different
Explore how intonation changes the meaning of a familiar phrase in the target language — for example, comparing a statement and a question using the same words
nodes.hinge_reason: Sound awareness is the foundation for all subsequent language comparison. Students who cannot perceive or imitate target language sounds cannot progress to noticing written features, word patterns or structural differences — all of which depend on being able to hear and reproduce the spoken language as a distinct system.

response_modes.reason: Sound awareness at Foundation level is built through repeated, varied exposure — songs, chants, tongue twisters, call-and-response. A single encounter with a sound pattern is insufficient; the sound must be encountered across multiple contexts and registers before students can reliably identify and imitate it.

success_criteria: Imitates at least two sounds or sound patterns from the target language with reasonable accuracy
Can identify at least one sound or pattern that is the same as English and one that is different

nodes.label: Noticing features of the writing system
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can notice that the target language has a writing system with features that may be similar to or different from English, and explore these with support.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one way the target language writing system is similar to or different from English — for example, shared letters, different characters, direction of writing.
nodes.typical_width: Explore features of the target language writing system alongside English — noticing shared letters or characters, differences in script or direction, and the relationship between written and spoken forms; participate in tracing, copying or labelling activities with target language text.
wider: Compare a short target language text with an English text — identify structural or visual differences such as spacing, punctuation conventions or script features
Explore borrowed words or expressions that appear in both languages in written form — notice what stays the same and what changes

response_modes.reason: Noticing writing system features requires scaffolded comparison — students at Foundation level need prompts to move from 'it looks different' to identifying specific features. Side-by-side text displays, teacher-led discussion and guided observation questions support this move from noticing to describing.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Background learners often have unexamined familiarity with the target language writing system from home exposure. Width investment here — particularly in exploring the relationship between the written and spoken forms they already know — builds metalinguistic awareness that is valuable across both languages.
success_criteria: Can point to or describe at least one feature of the target language writing system that is similar to English
Can point to or describe at least one feature that is different from English

nodes.label: Noticing word and sentence patterns
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can notice basic word and sentence patterns in the target language and compare them with English, using simple language to describe what they observe.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one pattern in how words or sentences are arranged in the target language — for example, word order, greeting structure, or a repeated phrase pattern — and compare it with English.
nodes.typical_width: Notice and discuss simple patterns in target language words and sentences — greetings, question forms, word order, common word combinations — and compare with equivalent English patterns; use teacher-supported metalanguage (word, sentence, same, different) to describe observations.
wider: Investigate a small set of words in both languages — for example, numbers, colours, family terms — and notice patterns in how they are formed or ordered differently
Compare a bilingual text (picture book, song, label) and identify matching words or structural patterns across the two languages

response_modes.reason: Noticing word and sentence patterns integrates sound awareness (node 1) and writing system observation (node 2) into a broader comparison of how the two languages work as systems. The teaching investment is in making comparisons explicit — inviting students to name what they notice rather than only experience it.

success_criteria: Can identify at least one pattern in target language word or sentence structure when prompted
Can compare the pattern with English, using simple language to describe the similarity or difference
